title: The 2026 oil shock, end to end: how we got here and how it ends
hook:
On the last day of February 2026, the first reports came through: American and Israeli aircraft were striking Iran. Within days Iran did the thing oil traders had war-gamed for decades and never quite believed would happen. It closed the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel through which a large share of India's crude arrives. A ceasefire in April bought a few weeks of relief. It fell apart in July. By October, tankers were being attacked again.

If you sat at a Mumbai trading desk through all of this, you lived through a relay race, not one shock. Oil ran the first leg, then US bond yields, then the rupee, then the government's budget arithmetic, then the RBI. And underneath all of it ran a daily tug of war between foreign funds selling Indian shares and domestic funds buying them.

Every earlier chapter explains one leg of that race. This one runs the whole thing. The question: how do the global forces and the Indian ones combine into the market we have today, and what would tell you, early, which way it breaks?
short: This is a supply-led oil shock, a pure tax on India with no growth upside, and it arrived with US yields at their highs, the worst pairing in our data.
The bill was passed down a chain: oil companies and airlines first, then the government through an excise cut, then the RBI through a currency defence that made money tight.
Domestic buyers have soaked up heavy foreign selling, which is why this drawdown looks like 2018, not 2020.
The base case is a grinding squeeze with wide gaps between winners and losers, and the regime is drifting from reflation towards stagflation.
The turn will come from the oil route and the rupee, not from Indian data. A crowded foreign short is not, on our data, a reliable signal that a rally is near.

sections.heading: Why this oil spike is a tax, not a boom
sections.html:
Start with the most important distinction in oil, because it decides everything that follows. Oil can rise for two very different reasons.

A demand-led rise happens when the world economy is booming and everyone wants more fuel. Oil gets dearer, but so does almost everything India sells: steel, chemicals, engineering goods, software services. Indian cyclicals can rise right alongside crude. A supply-led rise is the opposite. Nobody wants more oil; there is simply less of it, because a war, a sanction or a blocked shipping lane has cut it off. The price goes up and global growth goes down at the same time.

For a country that imports most of the oil it burns, a supply-led spike works exactly like a tax. Think of a family whose rent jumps while the salary stays put. Every extra rupee spent on fuel is a rupee not spent on cars or holidays, and it leaves the country altogether. Companies feel it as squeezed margins. The government feels it as subsidies and lost tax. The rupee feels it because more dollars are needed to buy the same oil.

That is what 2026 is. There is no booming world economy behind this rise. There is a war and a closed strait.

Here's the twist that matters most for investors. A good part of the price in a supply shock is a war premium: what traders pay for fear of losing barrels, over and above the barrels actually lost. Fear is priced quickly and unpriced even more quickly. When the route reopens or the damage turns out to be repairable, that premium can collapse within days. It happened in 1991 and it happened in 2019, as the stories below show. So this shock has a peculiar shape. It can grind on for months and then end abruptly, and the market will not wait for the data to confirm it.

sections.heading: The worst pairing: dear oil and dear money at once
sections.html:
Oil alone would have made this a bad year. What made it a dangerous one is a second force from outside: US government bond yields climbing to the highest levels in our data.

Why were US yields rising? Not because America was booming. The rise came mostly from what bond traders call the term premium, the extra return investors demand for locking money away for ten years when the future looks murky. An oil-driven inflation scare made that future murkier. So did a flood of borrowing: Washington's deficit, plus the bonds being sold to fund the AI data-centre build-out. More supply of bonds, more fear of inflation, higher yields.

For India, the US ten-year yield is the world's hurdle rate. When an American pension fund earns a high, safe return at home, it demands more from riskier markets. India also trades at a rich valuation compared with other emerging markets, and a rich valuation behaves like a long bond: it is a bet on profits far in the future, and those future profits are worth less today when the discount rate rises. Higher US yields therefore push foreign money out of India even if not a single Indian company's earnings change. They also strengthen the dollar, which pushes the rupee down, which makes oil dearer still in rupees.

Oil alone is a bad year for India. Oil plus rising US yields is how bad years turn into crises.
[[fig:1]]

The chart tells the whole relay in four panels, so read it top to bottom. Brent jumps when the war begins, dips with the spring ceasefire and climbs again after July. The US ten-year rises with it, which is the dangerous pairing in one picture. The rupee weakens to its record in July and then goes almost flat: that flatness is not calm, it is the RBI holding the line. And at the bottom, the Nifty has slid well off its January high.

sections.heading: Who pays the oil bill at home
sections.html:
Somebody in India has to pay for dearer oil. There are three candidates, and the order in which they pay is the story of this year.

  • The consumer at the pump. The simplest option politically is the hardest one: raise petrol and diesel prices and let households feel it. Pump prices in India are not reset daily with Brent, so this choice is made by the government and the state oil companies, not the market.
  • The oil companies. If pump prices stay frozen while crude rises, the state-owned fuel retailers sell at a loss on every litre. That gap is called an under-recovery, and it is really a hidden tax on their shareholders, a subsidy paid through the balance sheet instead of the budget.
  • The government. It can cut excise duty to give the oil companies room, at the cost of revenue, and it pays more fertiliser subsidy automatically, because fertiliser is made from imported gas.

This year the bill moved down that list. Pump prices stayed put after the war began, so the oil companies took the first hit, along with airlines, whose jet fuel bills rose at once. Then in late March 2026 the government slashed its special excise duty on petrol and scrapped the one on diesel to give the oil companies breathing room. The petroleum minister, Hardeep Singh Puri, conceded it was a big hit to revenue. New export duties on diesel and aviation fuel came alongside, to keep fuel at home.

So where does a government find that money? It usually protects the headline deficit target and slows something else, and the easiest line to slow quietly is capital spending: roads, railways, defence orders. That matters for every sector that has been riding public capex. The tell will not be in a speech. It will be in the monthly spending data.

There is one more consequence. Because pump prices were held, very little of the oil shock has reached the consumer price index yet. Inflation has started rising anyway, and the fuel part is still to come.

sections.heading: The external gap, and the corner the RBI was pushed into
sections.html:
Now follow the dollars. India buys far more from the world than it sells, and oil is the swing item. In a normal year India's two big structural earners, services exports and money sent home by Indians abroad, cover a normal oil bill. They cannot cover a spike.

The leftover gap has to be funded by foreign money coming in. Ideally that is patient money, companies building factories. But direct investment has weakened, and Indian households, who used to be large net savers, have been borrowing more, so their net surplus has thinned. That leaves the gap leaning on portfolio money: foreign funds buying shares and bonds, the most skittish money there is. When those funds leave, the rupee has nowhere to stand.

That put the RBI in a corner. Option one: let the rupee fall. That makes every imported barrel dearer, feeds inflation and can turn a slide into a stampede. Option two: defend it, by selling dollars from the reserves. But every dollar the RBI sells is paid for in rupees, which disappear from the banking system, so defending the currency automatically makes money scarcer. You cannot have free capital flows, a steady currency and cheap money all at once. Pick two.

The RBI picked the currency. In October 2026 it raised the repo rate for the first time in years, raised the cash reserve ratio, opened a dedicated dollar window for the oil companies so their huge purchases stopped hitting the open market, and tightened the rules on currency hedging. If the dollar window sounds familiar, it should: the RBI used the same trick in 2013.

The defence has worked, so far, on its own terms. The rupee peaked in July and has barely moved since. But the stress did not vanish. It moved from the currency market into the money market, where tighter liquidity now presses on lenders, home buyers and anyone who borrows to grow.

sections.heading: The tug of war that kept a floor under the market
sections.html:
So why no crash? Because of the most important structural change in Indian markets in a decade.

For most of the history of Indian equities, foreign investors set the direction. When they sold heavily, as in 2008, nobody big enough stood on the other side. That is no longer true. Domestic institutions, fed by the monthly SIP instalments of millions of salaried Indians, now own roughly as much of the market as foreigners do. This autumn foreign funds have been selling hard, and domestic funds have bought almost all of it.

There is a piece of market folklore worth killing here. Foreign investors are also heavily positioned for further falls in index futures. The old trader's rule says a crowd that short must eventually buy back, which sparks a rally. Our own data since 2022 says otherwise: a crowded foreign short has not reliably been followed by a rally. Positioning tells you the mood. It does not tell you the timing.

[[fig:2]]

The table lines this episode up against its two closest cousins, 2018 and 2022. Read across the rows and three things jump out. This year has the biggest oil move of the three. It has the smallest rupee move, because the rupee is being defended rather than allowed to find its level. And it has the calmest fear gauge, with the Nifty's worst fall so far shallower than in either earlier episode. 2022 still holds the record for the jump in US yields.

How should you read that calm? Generously, as proof that the domestic buyer has changed the shape of Indian drawdowns. Sceptically, as complacency: the floor holds only as long as the SIP money keeps coming. A long drawdown that pushes recent investors into losses, or deposit rates that start to look attractive, could slow that money. That is the scenario to fear, not the foreign selling itself.

sections.heading: Three ways this ends
sections.html:
Put the legs together and you get a regime. On published growth and inflation data India is in reflation, growth and inflation both rising. But this is a supply-led reflation, the bad kind for an oil importer, and the drift is towards stagflation: inflation still climbing as fuel finally reaches the index, while dear oil and tighter money slow activity. Both the global inputs and the Indian ones point that way. From here, three paths.

One: the route reopens. A durable ceasefire, or shipping through Hormuz restored. The war premium collapses, possibly in a few sessions. The rupee breathes, the RBI can stop tightening, and the sectors that were taxed by oil, airlines, paint makers, fuel retailers, carmakers, rally hardest. The market will move on the headline, not the data. This is the 1991 and 2019 ending.

Two: the grinding squeeze. Our base case. Oil stays high with periodic flare-ups, the RBI keeps holding the rupee and money stays tight, inflation broadens from fuel into everything else, and earnings estimates for oil users and heavy borrowers drift down quarter after quarter. The index goes sideways to lower, but the gap between winners and losers is wide. This is a stock picker's market, not a market for big index bets.

Three: escalation. Attacks spread, the second chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea is disrupted too, and oil spikes again. The RBI's reserves and forward commitments come under real strain, and it faces the choice it has avoided: let the rupee go or tighten much harder. The true tail is not oil itself but the floor giving way, domestic inflows stalling as losses mount.

One wildcard sits outside the Gulf. In mid-October the US paused a heavier round of penalty tariffs on buyers of Russian oil a day before it was due, while keeping the right to bring it back. That risk is deferred, not gone.

sections.heading: The signposts, in the order they should flash
sections.html:
Scenarios are only useful if you know what would tell them apart. Here is the watch list, roughly in the order the signals should arrive.

  1. The route. Tanker traffic through Hormuz, shipping insurance costs, attacks or their absence. This moves first and moves everything else. Watch the route, not the rhetoric.
  2. The rupee and the RBI's forward book. If the rupee stays flat while the RBI's promises to sell dollars in future keep growing, the defence is getting more expensive. A rupee that firms on its own is the opposite signal.
  3. The US ten-year. A retreat from the highs would take the second leg of the relay off India's back, even with oil still high.
  4. Monthly domestic fund flows. The floor. A sustained slowdown in SIP money matters more than any single week of foreign selling.
  5. The RBI's next statement. The vote split, and whether the liquidity paragraph talks about keeping money tight. A softer tone usually comes before any cut.
  6. Inflation and industrial output. Core inflation broadening, alongside slowing factory output, would confirm the turn to stagflation.
  7. Monthly capex spending. A quiet slowdown here is the sign the oil bill is being paid out of roads and railways.
Markets bottom when bad news stops getting worse, not when it stops.

Notice the order. The first signposts are global and fast, the last are Indian and slow, and that is exactly how the previous shocks ended: the outside pressure eased first and the domestic data improved months later. Notice also what is not on the list: GDP, quarterly earnings, or daily FII numbers. They describe the past, and in a supply shock the past is the least useful thing on your screen.

history.title: The night oil fell by a third
history.story:
When Saddam Hussein's army rolled into Kuwait in August 1990, oil roughly doubled within months, and India was hit twice over. Its import bill ballooned, and the money sent home by Indian workers in the Gulf dried up as they fled. Air India and the Indian Air Force flew well over a hundred thousand Indians out in one of the largest civilian evacuations ever. To secure Iraq's cooperation, the foreign minister, I.K. Gujral, went to Baghdad, where Saddam greeted him with a hug. The photograph went around the world.

Then, in January 1991, the American-led air war began. On early reports that it was going well, crude lost about a third of its price in a single session, its biggest one-day collapse ever. But India's damage outlasted the oil spike: within months its reserves ran dry and the RBI was flying gold abroad.
history.lesson: A war premium can vanish in a single session; the damage to a thin external buffer lasts much longer.

history.title: A window for the oil companies
history.story:
By late August 2013 the rupee was hitting a fresh record low almost every day, and the biggest buyers of dollars in the market were the three state oil companies, IOC, HPCL and BPCL, purchasing billions every month to pay for crude. Finance minister P. Chidambaram had already raised gold import duties repeatedly to cut the other big drain on dollars.

On the day the rupee hit its worst level, the RBI opened a special window to sell dollars to the oil companies directly, taking their demand out of the open market. The next day the rupee posted its biggest one-day gain in about a quarter of a century. A week later Raghuram Rajan arrived with his dollar deposit scheme for Indians abroad, and the crisis broke. Oil had not fallen at all.
history.lesson: Clever plumbing can end a currency crisis before oil turns, which is why the RBI reached for the same oil-company window in October 2026.

history.title: The press conference that sank the oil stocks
history.story:
By October 2018 Brent had climbed above eighty dollars, the rupee was at record lows and a large infrastructure lender, IL&FS, had just defaulted, freezing credit markets. On one October afternoon finance minister Arun Jaitley announced a cut in excise duty on petrol and diesel, and then asked the state oil companies to absorb a further cut themselves. Their shares fell about a fifth within hours.

The relief came from abroad. In November the US granted eight countries, India among them, waivers to keep buying some Iranian oil despite new sanctions. Oil had already started sliding, and it kept falling into the new year. The rupee and the market recovered with it, long before anything in India's own data improved.
history.lesson: In an oil-and-rupee squeeze the external variable turns first, and fuel retailers are the first to be asked to pay.

history.title: Abqaiq: the spike that evaporated
history.story:
Before dawn one September morning, drones and missiles slammed into Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq processing plant and the Khurais oilfield, knocking out more than half of the kingdom's output. When markets opened, Brent posted the biggest jump on record. Indian oil users sold off and the Nifty dipped.

Two days later the new Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, stood up and promised capacity would be largely restored by the end of the month. Aramco beat that deadline. Within a few weeks Brent was trading below where it had been before the attack, and the Nifty was higher than before the strike.
history.lesson: Ask whether the damage can be repaired quickly. If it can, the war premium is a fade, not a trend.

history.title: The bottom nobody rang
history.story:
Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and Brent spiked in March to levels unseen since 2008. In May, RBI governor Shaktikanta Das stunned the market with a hike between scheduled meetings. Weeks later finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman cut excise on petrol and diesel to cool pump prices. Across the ocean Jerome Powell's Fed was raising rates at the fastest pace in decades, and foreign investors sold Indian shares at a record clip.

And yet the Indian market bottomed that June. The Fed kept hiking for another year and the war was nowhere near over. What changed was the direction: oil eased off its spike, and the bad news stopped getting worse. Investors who waited for the all-clear bought much higher.
history.lesson: Markets turn on the rate of change, when bad news slows, not when it ends.

sowhat:
The base case is a grinding squeeze with wide dispersion: a market for choosing sectors, not betting on the index.

  • Be careful with oil consumers: airlines, paint makers, fuel retailers and carmakers lose on every link of the chain, and fuel retailers are the first to be asked to share the government's burden.
  • Be careful with wholesale-funded lenders such as non-bank finance companies and housing financiers, which feel tight money first.
  • Prefer banks with cheap, sticky deposits and externally linked loan books, which reprice upward first.
  • Expect staples to lag: they have lagged in every kind of oil shock in our history.
  • Commodity and capex exposure suits the regime while it holds, but treat that as a weak prior and watch monthly capex spending for a quiet slowdown.
  • Exporters gain from a weak rupee only if the RBI lets it go, and so far it has not. Richly valued IT and asset managers stay exposed to high US yields.

What would flip it: the oil route reopening, or the rupee firming without the RBI's help. Either would turn the oil losers into leaders, probably within days. A crowded foreign short, on its own, is not that signal.
